name: Atchan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Russell, Katherine R. 2026. Nasality in Atchan: Synchrony, diachrony and typology. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. 321 pp. eScholarship,https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5xq9m6nm(open access).
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 'The phonology of Atchan', §3.4 Tone, p. 65; §3.4.1.1 Nouns, p. 66; §3.5 Discussion, p. 86.
catalog_quote: Atchan makes use of two contrastive tones – Low (L) and High (H). Four distinct tone levels – High, Mid, Low, and SuperLow – and five contours – High-Low, High-Mid, Mid-Low, Low-SuperLow, and SuperLow-even lower – appear on the surface, all of which are attributable to the interaction of the two underlying tones and a number of regular tonal processes like High-tone spreading and plateauing (Lojenga, 1985; Bôle-Richard, 2008; Russell, 2023). [...] Per the near-identical distribution of tones across these different syllable shapes, I take the tone-bearing unit in Atchan to be the syllable, rather than a smaller unit like the mora. [...] Tone in Atchan bears a high functional load, serving to distinguish both lexical items and grammatical categories. The tone-bearing unit in Atchan is the syllable.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Atchan/Ebrié is a two-tone language (underlying /L/ and /H/; syllable = TBU; lexical melodies /L/, /H/, /LH/, /HL/ on monosyllabic noun roots, plus grammatical tone overlays and polar tones on verbs). The 50-page phonology chapter, and every other opened source, says nothing at all about word stress or accent; no stress position can be assigned. Most roots are monosyllabic CV (66% of 461 roots), verbs 92% monosyllabic.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal notes: some speakers merge /L/ and /LH/ noun classes; voiced obstruents are depressor consonants lowering L in nouns and all tones in verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Description is of lexical and postlexical tone on roots and words in isolation and in phrases (High-tone spreading, plateauing, phrase-position restrictions on surface tone); no word-level stress domain is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Atchan = Ebrié/Cámánncân/Tchaman (ebri1238, ISO ebr), data mainly from the Anono and Blockhauss (Ánonkwathé) villages inside Abidjan collected 2019-2025 with 15+ speakers; Russell's 'Atchan' is the same language as Glottolog's Ebrié. Mobio 2016 concerns the Bidjan-Nkyan variety (no separate glottocode).

new_statements.quote: Atchan is a Kwa language spoken by approximately 150,000 people in and around Abidjan in southern Côte d’Ivoire. In this paper, I describe aspects of the phonology of Atchan, including its consonant and vowel inventory, syllable structure, patterns of nasalisation, and lexical and grammatical tone. I provide examples from primary data collected in collaboration with native speakers of Atchan. This article offers the first comprehensive sketch of Atchan phonology in the literature.

Russell, Language and Linguistics Compass 17(4) article e12488, license CC-BY 4.0). The quoted abstract is present character-for-character inside message.abstract (<jats:p>..</jats:p>); exact-string match true. The abstract names the topics covered (consonant and vowel inventory, syllable structure, nasalisation, lexical and grammatical tone) and says nothing about stress or accent, so from the only text readable the work presents Atchan as a tone language with no stress statement; the compiler low confidence and has_stress_section=unknown are the right hedges because pp. 1-34 remain unr…
new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog record (classification tonal, from Russell 2026 dissertation: two contrastive tones L/H). The abstract adds nothing on stress. The same author's later and fuller treatment of the same material (Russell 2026 dissertation ch. 3 'The phonology of Atchan', pp. 36-87, held by the project) contains no word-stress or accent statement either; its only use of 'prominent positions' (p. 158) is defined morphosyntactically ('contexts in which the noun is not structurally dependent on another nominal head'), not prosodically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: From the abstract only: the article treats Atchan as a language with lexical and grammatical tone; the abstract lists the topics covered (segments, syllable structure, nasalisation, tone) and word stress/accent is not among them. Whether the body makes any explicit statement about stress could not be checked.
new_statements.identity_note: Atchan (also Ebrié, Cámán, Tchaman), spoken in and around Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire; the article and the dissertation describe the same speech community (author's primary fieldwork data); no dialect split is at issue.
